title: Saints Simon and Jude, Apostles
short_summary: Saints Simon and Jude were members of the Twelve Apostles. The New Testament gives only brief information about them: Simon is called the Cananaean or Zealot, while Jude is identified as distinct from Judas Iscariot and speaks once in John's account of the Last Supper.
key_facts: The Roman calendar celebrates Saints Simon and Jude together as a feast on October 28.
Simon appears in the apostolic lists as the Cananaean or the Zealot.
Jude is also called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark and is distinguished from Judas Iscariot.
A New Testament letter bears Jude's name, though its precise authorship has long been discussed.

sections.heading: Simon the Zealot
sections.body: Matthew and Mark call Simon the Cananaean, while Luke and Acts call him the Zealot. Both titles probably express zeal rather than securely identifying him with the later organized Zealot movement. He should not be confused with Simon Peter. Beyond his place among the Twelve, the New Testament records no individual words or actions by him.

sections.heading: Jude Thaddaeus
sections.body: The apostolic lists distinguish this Jude from Judas Iscariot, using forms such as Thaddaeus or Jude of James. In John's Gospel he asks why Jesus will reveal himself to the disciples and not to the world. Jesus answers by speaking of love, fidelity to his word, and the indwelling of the Father and Son. Christian devotion later made Jude a widely invoked patron in desperate circumstances.

sections.heading: The Letter of Jude
sections.body: The brief Letter of Jude warns Christians against teachers who distort grace and divide the community. It urges its readers to remain grounded in faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, and wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ. The letter identifies its author as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, but the relationship between this writer and the apostle has been interpreted in different ways.

sections.heading: Later traditions
sections.body: Traditions place Simon and Jude together as missionaries and martyrs in Persia, which accounts for their shared feast. Other ancient and medieval accounts assign them different fields of preaching and different deaths. Their relics are venerated together in Saint Peter's Basilica, but the historical details of their later lives cannot be reconstructed with certainty.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: The apostolic foundation
catholic_connection_sections.body: The Church honors even those apostles about whom little biography survives because their significance comes first from Christ's choice and commission. Together the Twelve represent the people gathered and sent by Jesus.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Unity without uniformity
catholic_connection_sections.body: Simon and Matthew, a zealously named disciple and a former tax collector, belonged to the same apostolic body. The Gospel's list shows Christ forming one communion from people with sharply different backgrounds.

historical_cautions: Do not identify Simon with the first-century Zealot party as a certain fact; the nickname may simply mean zealous.
The family relationships among the several New Testament figures named Judas, Jude, James, and Simon are disputed.
Missionary journeys and martyrdom in Persia belong to later traditions that vary substantially.
